title: Protection and Safety
blurb: Insurance and expected value, handling money shocks, fraud detection and giving effectively

terms.def: The average result if a choice were repeated many times: each outcome times its probability, added up.
terms.example: A 10% chance of losing $1,000 is an expected loss of $100.

terms.def: What you pay for insurance, monthly or yearly, whether or not you make a claim.
terms.example: $120 a month of health insurance is $1,440 a year in premiums.

terms.def: The amount you pay yourself on a claim before insurance pays. Higher deductibles mean lower premiums.
terms.example: A $1,000 deductible on a $4,000 repair: you pay $1,000 and the insurer pays $3,000.

terms.def: Covering small risks from your own savings instead of buying insurance for them. Fine for losses you can afford; never for ones that could ruin you.
terms.example: Skipping phone insurance and keeping $200 aside for a repair.

terms.def: Term life pays your family if you die during the term, replacing your income. Renters insurance covers your belongings and liability; homeowner's insurance also covers the building.
terms.example: A parent with young children buys 20-year term life cover worth ten times their salary.

cards.title: Trading a small cost for safety
cards.body: Insurance swaps a small certain cost (the premium) for protection from a large uncertain one. On average insurers take in more than they pay out, so insurance is a good deal for disasters you couldn't survive and usually a poor deal for small, affordable losses.

cards.title: Two policies
cards.body: Travel insurance costs $60 and covers a $3,000 medical emergency with a 1% chance: an expected payout of $30. It loses $30 on average, but a $3,000 bill could wreck the trip, so it can still be worth it. Phone insurance at $10 a month for a $150 repair that happens once every 3 years costs $360 for $150 of expected repairs: skip it.

cards.title: Comparing plans
cards.body: Expected value = sum of probability × outcome. Yearly cost of a plan = premiums + expected out-of-pocket costs (deductibles and co-pays). A higher deductible lowers the premium; choose it if your savings can cover it.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Picking the lowest premium without checking the deductible, or insuring every small item.

checks.prompt: There's a 2% chance of a $5,000 loss. What is the expected loss?
Plan A: premium $1,200, deductible $500. Plan B: premium $800, deductible $2,000. With one $3,000 claim, what does each cost you?

terms.def: Cash set aside for surprises like job loss or repairs, usually 3 to 6 months of essential costs, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.
terms.example: Essentials of $2,000 a month means a $6,000 to $12,000 fund.
terms.formula: months of cover = emergency fund ÷ monthly essentials

terms.def: Debt costing well above what savings earn, like credit cards at 20% or more, or payday loans. Avoiding and clearing it beats almost any investment.
terms.example: Paying off a 24% card is like earning a guaranteed 24%.

terms.def: Paying extra on the highest-rate debt first while paying the minimum on the rest. It costs the least interest. The snowball method pays the smallest balance first instead, for quick wins.
terms.example: Pay down the 24% card before the 7% car loan.

terms.def: In a crisis the cheapest order is usually: cut wants, use emergency cash, then low-cost credit, and only then sell investments or use high-interest debt. Selling investments after a crash locks in losses.
terms.example: Use savings before a 25% card, and avoid selling stocks right after a 30% fall.

cards.title: Getting through without damage
cards.body: A shock like a job loss, a medical bill and a rate rise arriving together tests the whole plan. The goal is to never miss a payment while keeping the long-run cost lowest: cut wants first, use emergency cash, keep high-interest debt as a last resort and avoid selling investments at the bottom.

cards.title: Three months without pay
cards.body: Essentials cost $2,500 a month and wants $800. The emergency fund holds $6,000. Cutting wants to $100 means drawing $2,600 a month, so the fund covers about 2.3 months. A cheap credit line covers the rest instead of a 26% card or selling shares that are down 20%.

cards.title: The numbers
cards.body: Months of cover = emergency fund ÷ monthly essentials. Cost of using credit ≈ balance × rate × years. Pay extra on the highest rate first (avalanche) to save the most interest.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Keeping no cash because investments earn more. When a shock hits you'd be forced to sell at a bad time or borrow at a high rate.

checks.prompt: Essential costs are $1,800 a month and the emergency fund holds $7,200. How many months of cover?
Which debt does the avalanche method pay off first?
checks.explanation: Highest rate first saves the most interest.

terms.def: Flagging something as bad when it was fine, like blocking a real customer's purchase.
terms.example: A traveller's card is declined at the airport.

terms.def: Missing something bad, like letting a fraudulent purchase through.
terms.example: A stolen card buys $900 of gift cards and nobody stops it.

terms.def: Of everything you flagged, the share that really was fraud.
terms.example: Flag 50 transactions and 40 are fraud: precision is 80%.

terms.def: Of all the real fraud, the share you caught.
terms.example: 60 frauds happened and you caught 40: recall is 67%.
terms.formula: recall = caught fraud ÷ all actual fraud

terms.def: Clues that raise the chance of fraud or a scam: urgent pressure, mismatched addresses, new devices, unusual places or amounts, requests for gift cards, codes or passwords.
terms.example: A first-time card used at 3 a.m. abroad for $2,000 of electronics.

terms.def: Fake messages pretending to be a trusted company to steal passwords, codes or money.
terms.example: A text saying your bank account is locked, with a link to a look-alike site.

terms.def: Long passwords, or passphrases of several random words, are far harder to crack than short complex ones. Turn on two-factor authentication for important accounts.
terms.example: 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is much stronger than 'P@ss1!'.

terms.def: Locking your credit report so nobody can open new credit in your name. It doesn't affect your score and you can lift it when you apply.
terms.example: After a data breach, freezing your credit stops a thief opening a card as you.

terms.def: Someone who moves stolen money for criminals, often recruited through fake job offers. It's illegal even if you were tricked.
terms.example: A 'job' paying you to deposit checks and wire 80% elsewhere is a money mule scam.

cards.title: Two kinds of mistake
cards.body: Every fraud filter trades two mistakes against each other: blocking good customers (false positives) and letting fraud through (false negatives). Precision measures how clean your blocks are; recall measures how much fraud you catch. The right balance depends on what each mistake costs.

cards.title: Block or approve?
cards.body: A $1,200 purchase with a 30% chance of fraud: approving it has an expected fraud loss of $360. Blocking it upsets a good customer 70% of the time, say $40 × 70% = $28. Block it. A $15 purchase with the same 30% chance: an expected loss of $4.50 against $28 of friction, so approve it.

cards.title: The measures
cards.body: Precision = caught fraud ÷ everything flagged. Recall = caught fraud ÷ all fraud. Block when chance of fraud × amount is bigger than chance it's genuine × the cost of a false alarm.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Blocking everything slightly unusual. You'd catch more fraud but anger so many customers that it costs more than the fraud. For your own accounts: never share codes, and check the sender before you click.

checks.prompt: You flagged 20 transactions and 15 were fraud. What is your precision?
There were 30 frauds in total and you caught 15. What is your recall?

terms.def: How much a charity spends to achieve one result, like one child vaccinated or one family housed. The best measure of value for money.
terms.example: Charity A spends $50 per child taught to read; Charity B spends $400. A does 8 times more per dollar.

terms.def: The share of spending on administration and fundraising. A low overhead isn't the same as high impact; good staff and measurement cost money.
terms.example: A charity with 25% overhead can still do more good per dollar than one with 5%.

terms.def: Giving investments that have risen in value instead of cash. You skip the capital gains tax and can still deduct the full value.
terms.example: Shares bought for $1,000 are now worth $5,000: give them and avoid tax on the $4,000 gain.

terms.def: Tax on the profit when you sell an investment for more than you paid. Investments held longer usually get a lower rate.
terms.example: Buy at $2,000 and sell at $5,000: tax is due on the $3,000 gain.

terms.def: An employer or donor adds money to your donation, often dollar for dollar, doubling its effect.
terms.example: You give $100 and your company matches $100: the charity gets $200.

terms.def: An account you give to now, taking the deduction this year, then recommend grants to charities later.
terms.example: Put in $5,000 during a high-income year and grant it out over five years.

cards.title: Good per dollar
cards.body: Effective giving asks how much good each dollar does. Compare charities by cost per outcome, not by how low their overhead is. Then make the money go further: tax deductions, giving appreciated shares instead of cash, and matching gifts all stretch the same budget.

cards.title: Stretching $1,000
cards.body: You're in the 24% bracket. A $1,000 cash gift saves $240 of tax, so it costs you $760. Giving $1,000 of shares you bought for $400 also avoids tax on the $600 gain, about $90 at 15%, so it costs about $670. Add a dollar-for-dollar employer match and the charity gets $2,000.

cards.title: The maths
cards.body: Real cost of a deductible gift = gift × (1 − marginal tax rate). Shares also save the capital gains rate × the gain. Results delivered = money reaching the charity ÷ cost per outcome.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Picking charities by lowest overhead or the most emotional story. Ask for the cost per result, and check a charity is registered before you give.

checks.prompt: In the 22% bracket, what does a $500 deductible donation really cost you?
Charity A helps one person for $200 and Charity B for $1,000. With the same budget, which helps more people?
checks.explanation: A helps 5 times as many people per dollar.
